title: New craft beer made from Japanese udon noodles celebrates centuries of Mizusawa food culture
description: Noodles loved by hot spring fans and temple pilgrims become a very unique brew. Like with all Japanese noodles, you don’t cut udon when eating it. You simply pick up a mouthful of noodles with your chopsticks, take a bite, and slurp up the rest. However, udon does get cut during the production process, so […]
content:
Noodles loved by hot spring fans and temple pilgrims become a very unique brew.

Like with all Japanese noodles, you don’t cut udon when eating it. You simply pick up a mouthful of noodles with your chopsticks, take a bite, and slurp up the rest.

However, udon does get cut during the production process, so that the noodles in each batch will have a uniform length. This means that noodle makers, whether individual restaurants or supplier factories, end up udon noodle scraps. These usually get tossed out, since they’re too short to make extra noodles out of, but as of this month some of that extra udon is getting made into craft beer.

Mizusawa 15 Udon Ale takes the first part of its name from Mizusawa, a district of the town of Shibukawa, Gunma Prefecture. Shibukawa has three claims to fame: Mizusawa Kanon Temple, the hot springs of the town’s Ikaho Onsen district, and the Mizusawa udon noodles that visitors to both have been eating for hundreds of years. Made with a blend of different types of locally grown wheat and pure water sourced from Mount Mizusawa and Mount Haruna, Mizusawa udon noodles are said to have been first made by monks at the temple, and then popularized further at restaurants and inns along the approach that pilgrims would patronize.

▼ Gate of Mizusawa Kanon Temple

Recently, the Shibukawa Ikaho Onsen Tourism Association approached sustainable design company consultancy Odoriji for help developing a beer that would represent Mizusawa’s local food culture and traditions. Incorporating Mizusawa udon was the obvious choice, but it took some extra thinking to figure out how to make that happen. Though the noodles are made with high-quality wheat, the noodle scraps won’t ferment without some extra help. First they’re crushed and placed in carefully temperature-controlled hot water that malt enzymes are also introduced to. This converts the udon noodles’ starches into sugars which can then be used in the fermentation and brewing process, which is performed by Tokyo-based craft brewer Sakatsugi Brewing.

The result is a 5-percent ABV ale that Odoriji describes as having an immediate gentle sweetness with a touch of fruitiness coming on afterwards, but which doesn’t linger so long as to prevent a refreshingly crisp, clean finish. Naturally, they recommend pairing it with Mizusawa udon, as well as tempura, a popular accompaniment for the noodles.

As for the “15,” that’s in reference to Route 15, the road leading to Mizusawa Kanon Temple which includes such a dense cluster of noodle restaurants in one part that’s it’s earned the nickname “Mizusawa Udon Street.”

▼ The label artwork depicts a section of the winding road as an undulating udon noodle.

Mizusawa 15 Udon Ale went on sale just this month on October 10, and is being offered through Odoriji’s online shop in two, four, and six-can bundles. It’s also being served at select restaurants in Mizusawa and Ikaho (listed here). Quantities are limited, as the beer is still in its test-marketing stage, but hopefully it’ll make its way to other parts of Japan too soon.

Source: PR Times, Visit Gunma

title: This shrine in Japan invites you to hit and kick its god of poverty statue for good luck [Photos]
description: Instead of praying to the binbogami, you’re supposed to fight him off. When visiting a shrine in Japan, the standard custom is to put a coin in the offering box, bow twice, clap your hand twice, say a quick, silent prayer, and then bow once more. So we were very surprised when we discovered a […]
content:
Instead of praying to the binbogami, you’re supposed to fight him off.

When visiting a shrine in Japan, the standard custom is to put a coin in the offering box, bow twice, clap your hand twice, say a quick, silent prayer, and then bow once more.

So we were very surprised when we discovered a shrine in Nagano Prefecture where instead of bowing and clapping, you’re supposed to strike and kick the statue of its god instead.

The shrine, located in the town of Chino, can’t be seen from the street. Instead, you’ll need to look for Hakko Park (“Fermentation Park”), a sort of local products and museum managed by miso maker Marui Ito Shoten.

Inside the facility you can see the giant wooden barrels used for the traditional miso-making process. They are impressive-looking, but the real sight to see is at the back of the building, where you’ll find signs directing you towards the passageway to Binbogami Shrine.

▼ Binbogami Shrine would usually be written in Japanese as 貧乏神神社, but since the language can also be read from right to left, the signs here render it as 社神神乏貧.

Even on a sunny afternoon, the shrine is shadowy, making it feel like you’ve wandered into a mysterious parallel world.

But where things get really strange is the shrine’s statue of a binbogami, or “god of poverty.”

An one-horned creature with a gaunt physique and eyes shaped like gold coins, binbogami have appeared in Japanese legends and folklore since the 13th century. They’re said to be particularly fond of the smell of miso, using their tattered fans to waft the aroma of the staple food towards themselves to better savor the scent.

Of course, no one wants a god of poverty hanging around, especially since they’re said to not only trigger financial losses, but general unhappiness and lack of success. One way of getting rid of binbogami is supposed to be to prepare a tray of baked miso, carry it through your home, and then toss it into a river, so that the spirit will follow it into the waterway and drift away from your dwelling.

But at Binbogami Shrine, they have a different, more visceral method. First you put a 100-yen coin in the collection pot…

…then you pick up a “poverty stick”…

…and then you give the god of poverty three sturdy whacks!

No more than three, though. After that, you have to set the stick down…because it’s time to kick the god three times too!

This process is described on the signs posted inside the shrine, which is a satellite branch of Nagano’s Suwa Shrine, which itself traces its history back to the 7th century. The signs also explain the final part of the ritual to drive away the god of poverty, which is to throw beans at the statue, giving it some overlap with the annual Setsubun bean-throwing festival in which launched legumes are said to repeal demons and misfortune. For extra effectiveness, calling out something like “Binbogami, begone!” or “Damn you!” during your toss is recommended.

Thankfully, Binbogami Shrine keeps a tray of beans ready…

…so we pelted the god of poverty with a small handful of them.

Pasted to the walls of the enclave that surrounds the binbogami are papers emblazoned with undesirables such as “my jerk boss,” “drunken middle-aged guys,” and “body fat,” as well as desired outcomes such as “Sickness, be gone!” and “Win the lottery.”

That mixture might seem a little contradictory, but the general sense is that by hitting, kicking, and throwing beans at the god of poverty, you’ll get him to leave you alone for a while so that bad things will stop happening to you, leaving more space for good fortune in your life instead.

The shrine has a way to help call more good luck into you life too, in the form of an otafuku mask, also called an okame mask.

Since these are generally a symbol of happiness and good fortune, there’s no more hitting or kicking to be done, and instead you’re supposed to gently rub or pat the mask.

We’ve gone to a lot of shrines in our travels across Japan, but Binbogami Shrine stands out as a completely unique experience. If you’re headed there, though, there’s an important warning to keep in mind: While striking and kicking the statue is encouraged, the shrine also cautions to not hit the binbogami too hard.

On a secular level, this helps keep the statue in good repair for the next visitors, but the shrine also says that too much ferocity directed at the statue will bounce back on you and actually increase your bad luck, so be careful not to overdo it.

Location information
Binbogami Shrine / 貧乏神神社
Located within Haako Park / 発酵パーク
Address: Nagano-ken, Chino-shi, Miyagawa 4529
長野県茅野市宮川4529
Open 9 a.m.-7 p.m.

title: Town in Kanagawa struggling with violent gang of monkeys
description: Problematic monkeys appear to be moving into abandoned homes. Of course, it’s great to be involved in protecting the environment, but recently I can’t shake the feeling that people in Japan are increasingly in need of being protected from the environment. Year after year, bears have been venturing deeper into inhabited and even somewhat urban […]
content:
Problematic monkeys appear to be moving into abandoned homes.

Of course, it’s great to be involved in protecting the environment, but recently I can’t shake the feeling that people in Japan are increasingly in need of being protected from the environment. Year after year, bears have been venturing deeper into inhabited and even somewhat urban areas, resulting in violence and damage. Now, monkeys are beginning to take over the streets too.

That’s the case in the town of Yugawara in Kanagawa Prefecture, where a troop of Japanese macaques has been involved in numerous incidents of assaults, loitering, theft, harassment, and vandalism throughout the once tranquil streets of this popular hot spring area.

Yugawara has had monkeys roaming around the area since 1955, but one troop in particular, dubbed “T1”, is the first to have begun acting like a bunch of juvenile delinquents. This gang of 20 simians is believed to have been responsible for 6,054 incidents in 2025 alone.

▼ A news report with numerous videos of monkeys walking around like they own the place

Last month, a man in his 40s was attacked and bitten by one, marking the first time anyone’s ever been bitten by a monkey there. It is unclear why these monkeys are suddenly turning against people, but the head of a local monkey control center believes some event in the past must have triggered their recent rash of violent, anti-social behavior.

Regardless, the animals are clearly well-accustomed to living around town. They can be seen sitting around on roadsides and aren’t even spooked by an ambulance speeding by with its siren on. Some experts suspect they’ve traded in their usual shelter of treetops for far more comfy abandoned houses on the edge of town, the result of Japan’s rampant population decline. A survey in 2024 found 433 such homes in Yugawara.

In an effort to learn more about their behavior, the monkey control center managed to attach GPS trackers to two alpha males in the troop. Using these, they’ll also be able to dispatch “monkey removal teams” who use firecrackers to shoo away the primates before they do any harm. However, given the rate at which they’ve been acclimatizing themselves, the effectiveness of this may not last long.

Yuagawara’s economy relies heavily on tourism, with visitors coming to the town for its hot springs and traditional ryokan inns, as well as orange-picking at its orchards in late autumn. But residents are worried that people will stay away for fear of their own safety against the aggressive macaques. Readers of the news online sympathized with them, and comments expressed a desire for more to be done about animal control in general.

“6,000 in one year?! And those are just the reported cases.”
“If we don’t make the monkeys fear us, both sides will suffer.”
“They’re learning that humans scare easily.”
“I was kicked in the back by one of those. I wasn’t seriously hurt, but they are crazy strong.”
“Some monkeys were causing trouble around my farm, so I got a hunter to shoot at them and they never came back. They need to be taught to fear humans.”
“At least bears hibernate in the winter.”
“If we re-introduce wolves to Japan, they can help control the population of monkeys and deer.”

I guess wolves might help, but honestly, at the rate things are going it seems very likely they’d just start attacking people and encroaching on inhabited areas too. Then we’d have bears, boars, monkeys, wolves, and the occasional escaped crocodile to deal with in our daily lives.

In the case of T1, however, if these problems persist, it’s likely they will be officially classified as an “unmanageable troop.” This means the monkeys have become irrevocably adapted to inhabited areas and require live trapping and euthanizing of members until the troop has been completely broken up.

Not an ideal solution, since they are just monkeys being monkeys, but without the proper financial support to create a way to handle problems like this, the people whose livelihoods are threatened by them will have to do what it takes to solve it.

Source: FNN Online Prime, YouTube/フジテレビ 報道【公式】

title: What’s it like to stay in a Japanese container hotel?
description: We spend the night in the new rising-star class of hotels in Japan. There’s a new class of travel accommodation that’s been rising in popularity in Japan recently: the container hotel. Not to be confused with capsule hotels, in which you rent a slot in a wall of sleeping compartments for the night, container hotels […]
content:
We spend the night in the new rising-star class of hotels in Japan.

There’s a new class of travel accommodation that’s been rising in popularity in Japan recently: the container hotel. Not to be confused with capsule hotels, in which you rent a slot in a wall of sleeping compartments for the night, container hotels give you an actual private room…but that room in enclosed within what’s essentially a converted shipping container.

Container hotels tend to be less expensive than conventional lodgings, but do those saving come at the cost of cramped, maybe even claustrophobic discomfort? To find out, we sent our Japanese-language reporter Takashi Harada to container hotel Cradle Cabin, located in the city of Tateyama in Chiba Prefecture, to spend the night.

As you can see, each container is narrow enough to fit inside a parking space. Granted, these are parking spaces wide enough to accommodate shipping trucks, but still, it doesn’t seem like a lot of left-to-right space from the outside. Things didn’t look any more encouraging when Takashi opened the door to his room, and he inwardly groaned a little at how narrow the layout appeared.

However, after stepping past the entry area, he discovered a surprisingly well-designed interior with all the space he really needed.

Sure, the dimensions are still cozy, but this is pretty much as much space as you get in Japan’s budget-friendly “business hotels.” As for why the area just inside the door seems so narrow, that’s because the container has its own self-contained bathroom and shower.

This was also a pleasant surprise, as Takashi had been bracing himself for the possibility that container hotels would only have a communal restroom and bathing facility. Instead, he had a fully private setup, again comparable to what you’ll find in most regular budget-priced Japanese hotels, including a nice washlet-type toilet.

Continuing to check for places Cradle Cabin might have cut corners, he next checked the bed. Once again, though, his worries were misplaced. The mattress was soft but supportive, and the housekeeping staff had laid out two pillows of differing firmness for him to pick from.

Neatly arranged on and in the desk were a smart TV, clock, phone, hot water kettle, coffee mugs, hair dryer, and tissue box, again, the expected array of niceties for a Japanese hotel…

…and next to the desk was a microwave, a rarity in Japanese hotel rooms, and a nicely sized refrigerator with a freezer compartment too.

Peeking into the shower again, Takashi confirmed that even the provided soap and shampoo are up to scratch, as they’re made by Pola, a well-respected Japanese brand…

…and while you have to grab them from the check-in desk, Cradle Cabin provides all sorts of toiletries like towels, slippers, cotton pads, razors, hair brushes, as well as complimentary coffee and green tea.

In short, this container hotel isn’t missing anything that you’d expect from a regular hotel, and considering the 8,080 yen (US$51) that Takashi was paying for the night, the quality of those amenities were actually above what you usually get in that price range.

But now for the big question: Does staying in a container hotel trigger a claustrophobia attack? Not in Takashi’s case. Yes, the lack of windows can feel a little strange at first, but once he was settled in for the night, lying down in bed and relaxing while watching TV, he stopped being really conscious of being surrounded by four solid walls. Later, after he turned off the lights and closed his eyes, he enjoyed a deep, restful sleep. There was no unwanted ambient light seeping into the room to wake him up in the early morning, and since none of his container’s walls were in contact with those of any other guests, there wasn’t any sound coming through them either.

That said, when Takashi stepped out of his container the next morning, he did feel acutely aware of how wide open the outside world is, and if your travel style involves spending a couple hours in the afternoon just relaxing in your room, the lack of exterior views might start to feel a little oppressive. But as a place to spend the night, capsule hotels are surprisingly comfortable, and now that Takashi has stayed in one, he’d have no worries about staying in another, like maybe Cradle Cabin’s new location it’s planning to open soon in Nishitokyo, west of downtown Tokyo.

Related: Cradle Cabin Tateyama

title: New Tokyo facility promises to make you feel reborn, time in the womb and all [Photos]
description: Sauna Mother promises to provide the sense of calming security felt by a newborn baby. A good sauna session should be refreshing, the sort of thing that lets you shed the stress from the myriad pressures and responsibilities of adult life. Ideally, you should emerge feeling reborn, and if you think the best way to […]
content:
Sauna Mother promises to provide the sense of calming security felt by a newborn baby.

A good sauna session should be refreshing, the sort of thing that lets you shed the stress from the myriad pressures and responsibilities of adult life. Ideally, you should emerge feeling reborn, and if you think the best way to do so is by recreating your time in the womb, and the immediate aftermath of your emergence. Tokyo has got a place for you.

Opening soon in the downtown Roppongi neighborhood is Sauna Mother, which touts itself as a place where you can “stop being an adult for two hours.” Rather than indulge in such grade-school level nostalgia as eating a bunch of ice cream or playing on a swing set, though, Sauna Mother takes customers all the way back to the prenatal stage of childhood. For example, instead of a regular old sauna, the facility has a Uterus Sauna, which reproduces the sensations of being in the womb through fleshy red lighting, muffled sounds, and a scent its designers say is evocative of the smell of a mother’s skin. You can even have your photo taken to be placed on your “rebirth certificate” that Sauna Mother provides.

Sauna Mother mercifully passes on reenacting the dramatic intensity of the birthing procedure itself, so after emerging from the Uterus Sauna you’ll proceed to the Newborn Bath, a cold-water bath meant as an allegory to the initial rinsing of birthing fluids off of a newborn child.

Subsequently, you’ll be warmed back up again in the Mother’s Lap Shower, for which guests are propped on a seat shaped like a woman’s torso and thighs.

Finally, there’s perhaps the most visually impactful part of the experience, the Mother Sofa, where guests are cradled, rocked, and watched over.

The first two parts of that come from a reclining sofa with carefully calculated contours meant to eliminate excess pressure on any point of the body while you lie there and the surface sways back and forth, at one of three selectable speeds, like a mother rocking her baby to sleep. As for being watched over…

…projected above you is the countenance of one of four motherly figures, either Izanami, the Shinto mother goddess, the Two-Dimensional Mother (who looks sort of like a Ghilbi-version of classic anime character Sazae-san), the Impressionism-inspired Art Mother, or the Mythology Mother.

The goal of all this, Sauna Mother says, is to provide guests with “the sense of security they felt as newborns,” which will have them feeling invigorated when their session ends. The possibility that this unique sauna experience will instead scare the hell out of people and leave them debilitatingly terrified is something the management doesn’t address in its promotional materials, but no one can accuse Sauna Mother of being anything less than upfront about what customers can expect, so the facility is unlikely to have any customers who are themselves uncomfortable with the aesthetics.

Sauna Mother says it’s on track for its grand opening at the end of this month, with reservations set to open through its website in mid-October. The price for a one-person, two-hour session is listed at 8,500 yen (US$54), but there are discounts for group sessions of two, three, or four people, or maybe they should be reffered to as twins, triplets, and quadruplets.

title: Japan’s newest anime figure crane game prize may also be the world’s weirdest hanger [Photos]
description: There are two reasons this figure is posed that way. Prizes for UFO catchers/crane games in Japan tend to fall into one of two categories. In one you have stuff that you don’t really need, but which is awesome to have, like a giant Dragon Quest Shadow Slime plushie. Then you have the other group, […]
content:
There are two reasons this figure is posed that way.

Prizes for UFO catchers/crane games in Japan tend to fall into one of two categories. In one you have stuff that you don’t really need, but which is awesome to have, like a giant Dragon Quest Shadow Slime plushie. Then you have the other group, stuff that’s desirable because it serves some sort of practical purpose, like skin care packs or sweet potatoes.

At first glance, this figure of Yujiro Hanma, from manga/anime franchise Baki the Grappler, might seem like it’s in the first category. After all, anime figures don’t do anything other than sit on the shelf and look cool, right?

Ah, but wait a second – there’s no base for the figure, so how is it even supposed to sit on your shelf? The answer is that it isn’t, because this isn’t any ordinary anime figure, it’s an anime figure that’s also a clothes hanger.

Baki, which started its still-ongoing manga run in 1991, is a martial arts series, and one that falls into a very specific niche of the genre. On the one hand, it’s got no interest in the sort of metaphysical/science fiction-elements of Street Fighter or Dragon Ball, so you won’t see Yujiro or the other fighters throwing fireballs or energy blasts at each other. At the same time, author and artist Keisuke Itagaki isn’t trying to tell a grounded, realistic story either. The result is a series filled with characters with unabashedly pulling off technically possible but highly implausible feats of physical prowess, and one that’s over the top by an especially wide margin is Yujiro’s ability to do the splits with a limberness far beyond what one would reasonably expect of someone with that much muscle mass in his lower body.

gym biceps back + baki tshirt today

goal : yujiro splits pic.twitter.com/lZegOj0pfM

— yassin (@212Hanma) February 13, 2026

Height is usually the key measurement for anime figures, but understandably manufacturer Bandai is instead listing the it’s width instead, which is 50 centimeters (19.7 inches), so it seems like Yujiro should be able to hold up jackets and shirts as well as the tank tops he’s supporting in the preview photos.

The Yujiro Hanma hanger is appearing in Japanese arcade crane games stocked by Bandai Spirits as of October 6.

title: Pizza Hut in Japan now serves spicy glass noodle pizza
description: No fewer than five nations are involved in the Malatang Pizza. Pizza Hut Japan has always been an example of culinary cross-culturalism, but it’s become even more enthusiastically eclectic with some of its recent offerings, such as the chrysanthemum tsukimi and drinkable curry pizzas we saw earlier in the year. Now the chain has yet […]
content:
No fewer than five nations are involved in the Malatang Pizza.

Pizza Hut Japan has always been an example of culinary cross-culturalism, but it’s become even more enthusiastically eclectic with some of its recent offerings, such as the chrysanthemum tsukimi and drinkable curry pizzas we saw earlier in the year. Now the chain has yet another innovation in their ovens with the launch of the Malatang Pizza.

The inspiration comes from the spicy Chinese noodle hot pot style called malatang, which originated in the Sichuan region.

Instead of Pizza Hut’s standard tomato sauce, the Malatang Pizza uses a mixture of Sichuan peppercorns and chili oil for a tinglingly spicy blend.

Also part of the package are sliced pork, wood ear mushrooms (called kikurage in Japanese), and what Pizza Hut describes as “Korean-style glass noodles.”

Tying everything together is a two-cheese blend of mozzarella and gouda, resulting in a mix of Chinese, Korean, and Italian elements, all offered by the Japanese arm of an American restaurant chain.

Of course, malatang isn’t a dish that Pizza Hut has a lot of first-hand experience with, so the new pizza was developed under the guidance of Chipao Maratan, a popular malatang specialty restaurant chain with branches in eastern, northern, and central Japan which regularly have long lines of local customers waiting to get in.

In addition to the standard Malatang Pizza (which starts at 880 yen (US$5.50) for a small, Pizza Hut also has a fancier Seafood Malatang Pizza (from 1,490 yen) with shrimp and squid…

…plus a Vegetable Malatang Pizza (from 1,310 yen) with asparagus and corn, proving once again that there is no way of completely dissuading Japan from putting corn on pizza.

The Malatang Pizza joined the Pizza Hut Japan menu on October 8 and will be available until November 4.

content:
Goodness gracious, great balls of rice and beef!

Komeda Coffee is a nationwide chain of coffee shops that’s earned a reputation as practitioners of “reverse fraud” (gyakusagi). 

More often than not, when looking at a restaurant’s menu, you’ll see images of towering burgers and overflowing fries, only to be greeted with a pale imitation of that on your plate. At Komeda, however, the opposite is more likely to happen. What might appear a modest pork cutlet sandwich on the menu turns out to be a huge feast you’ll have trouble finishing. It’s a phenomenon so sadly rare, we don’t even really have a good English term for it. I guess you could call it a “rip-on” maybe?

One example of this was Komeda’s Kome-Gyu from 2020. This was a burger with shredded beef short rib slathered in chili-mustard sauce and topped with shredded cabbage. It came in three sizes, with the largest having nearly a pound of beef.

It was a hugely popular item and cemented Komeda’s status as a reverse fraudster, because those burgers were way more hearty than even our photo above lets on. However, when they re-released Kome-Gyu on 9 September, there wasn’t much buzz. In fact, even our own gourmet writer Mr. Sato was unaware until they tweeted about it on 3 October.

The tweet quickly went viral, racking up over 10,000 likes and a million views as word of Kome-Gyu’s return spread like wildfire. Part of the reason no one noticed was that this Kome-Gyu wasn’t sold at Komeda Coffee but at their spin-off chain Komeya no Taro that specializes in onigiri rice balls. As such, this Kome-Gyu is not a burger but an onigiri.

There’s certainly nothing wrong with that, so Mr. Sato hurried over to Komeya no Taro to try it and some other offerings out. There are only three locations in the country, two in Saitama and, luckily for him, one nearby in Shinjuku, Tokyo.

This was our reporter’s first trip there, and he scanned the menu to get a sense of things. Komeya no Taro sells a decent variety of rice balls, each in “mini” or “regular” sizes. The prices also range a bit, from 190 yen ($US1.20) for a Salted Rice Ball to the Eel Rice Ball for 770 yen ($4.90).

Mr. Sato decided to buy three on this trip. First, he bought a regular size Salted Rice Ball for 310 yen. There was nothing particularly special about this onigiri, as it was just salt and rice. In fact, the only reason our writer bought this was because a Japanese word for “rice” is “kome” and “da” is the casual form of the “to be” verb and could be translated as “it’s,” which means this rice ball gave him license to write:

▼ “Komeda kome da!”

Having gotten that out of his system, Mr. Sato moved on to his next onigiri. The Miso Pork Tenderloin Rice Ball was easily the most eye-catching item on the menu and sold for 510 yen in its regular size.

The breaded and fried pork tenderloin cutlet jutted out the top to such a degree it didn’t seem right to even call it a rice ball. It had a drizzling of miso sauce down the side, like an erupting volcano.

Cutting it in half revealed that there wasn’t much pork inside the onigiri itself. Still, it can’t really be said that Komeya no Taro was being chintzy with the meat. It was more just arranged oddly.

Finally, it was time for the main event of the Kome-Gyu Rice Ball, which sells in a regular for 640 yen.

Looking at it, Mr. Sato didn’t get a sense of Komeda’s reverse fraud. It was a perfectly average-looking onigiri in terms of size, though the amount of beef appeared plentiful as it seemed to overflow from the top.

He tried cutting it open to get a better sense of what it contained, but it was so crumbly it more or less fell apart in the process.

It had a good amount of meat, but again, not so much that our writer would describe it as a case of reverse fraud. It all seemed perfectly reasonable. It did excel in the taste department, however. The taste of the sauce was outstanding and complemented the rice as well as the meat.

It made Mr. Sato realize that this kind of meat’s natural partner is rice rather than buns. It all went so well together that as he ate, he wished Komeda would just cut to the chase and release a proper gyudon beef bowl with these ingredients. Perhaps they will one day, and perhaps there was no reverse fraud this time because they’re saving it for Kome-Gyu’s final form.

title: Free-flowing cocktails, natural onsen water, and custom pillows make this Osaka hotel a steal
description: Room-only stays usually mean no perks, but this hotel throws them at you, all in the name of having a good sleep. There is a type of accommodation for all kinds of traveler, be it a gorgeous mountain retreat or a city-based hub for neighborhood exploration. For some people, accommodation means just having a comfortable […]
content:
Room-only stays usually mean no perks, but this hotel throws them at you, all in the name of having a good sleep.

There is a type of accommodation for all kinds of traveler, be it a gorgeous mountain retreat or a city-based hub for neighborhood exploration. For some people, accommodation means just having a comfortable place to pass the night, spending the rest of the time out and about, so they tend to go for places that offer room-only stays instead of hunting for one that has a decent breakfast menu. However, we were recently invited to a trial stay at Super Hotel Premier Osaka Hommachi Ekimae, where even with a room-only stay, alcohol, a hot spring, and amenities are all included completely free of charge.

Being located right next to Osaka’s Hommachi Station, served by the Osaka Metro Midosuji Line, Yotsubashi Line, and Chuo Line, means that it is incredibly convenient for any exploring you want to do while spending time in the city. Additionally, the popular shopping district of Shinsaibashi is well within walking distance, and the area around Hommachi Station is full of places to eat and drink.

Going up to the second floor, we were met with the front desk located inside a clean lobby, and a faint aroma drifted through the air.

Check-in is possible using a QR code for the tech-savvy, but it’s just as possible to complete the procedures at the counter, where the receptionist explains various things about the hotel:

  • You can choose the softness and height of your pillow.
  • Lobby coffee and tea are available to drink 24 hours a day.
  • You can enjoy a welcome bar starting in the evening.
  • There is a hot spring.
  • You can borrow nightwear developed in-house.
  • Women receive five skincare amenities.

All of this for just a room-only stay? It’s truly hard to believe, so we couldn’t wait to experience it for ourselves.

First, we meandered over to the coffee and tea provisions, which you are apparently allowed to bring into your room too.

▼ The tea bags were from TEARTH, with an extensive lineup.

However, the highlight is the welcome bar opening in the evening, where various types of alcohol are set out, and you can freely make and enjoy your own cocktails.

In the case you want to avoid alcohol, soft drinks are also well-stocked, and even small snacks like nuts and dried fruits are provided. It was even mentioned that it was possible to bring in food from the outside to enjoy with your drinks.

A drink in hand while idly gazing at the cityscape and flowing lights of cars… it was utter bliss.

There is a shower in the room, but since we were told about it, we had to check out the natural hot spring, which you can check the crowdedness of from the television in your room.

▼ Photograph taken with permission.

The hot water is brought in from the source spring Naniwa Onsen, and felt like a simple hot spring, but explanations in the bathing area introduced it as having beautifying and rejuvenating effects. Being able to stretch out your legs and thoroughly warm up your body, tired from traveling, is something to be extremely grateful for. After getting out of the bath, you’ll have the opportunity to enjoy the amenities on offer and ReFa hairdryers.

Of course, on the way back to your room you should also stop off at the lobby for some herbal tea.

To truly make your night special, you need to select your own custom pillow from the selection of various firmnesses and heights lined up in the lobby. We went for the Mochi-Fuwa Ladies Pillow, a collaboration with custom-made pillow maker Jibun Makura, and true to its name is apparently exclusively for women.

Furthermore, the mattress and pajamas are also Super Hotel originals, which have come about as a result of their exploration of good sleep in their partnership with universities under the name Good Sleep Research Institute (Gussuri Kenkyujo).

From the aroma in the lobby, the hot spring, the water, the duvet, to the room lighting, everything is specifically designed to help guests get a good sleep. Thanks to that, we fell sound asleep right through until morning.

▼ We couldn’t wait to test out our custom pillow.

Breakfast was at the Organic Table restaurant on the second floor for an extra fee of 1,500 yen (US$9.49), although there are also breakfast (and dinner) plans available. The buffet menu had plenty of vegetables and side dishes, making for a grand display of variety. There were even popular Osaka items like takoyaki and nikusui (beef soup), which are sure to please tourists.

Perhaps because we woke up feeling completely refreshed, our appetites were strong, and we thoroughly enjoyed the meal. We highly recommend this breakfast for anyone who wants a substantial meal to start the day.

Check-out was at 11:00 a.m., and with the room key being a passcode, there was nothing special to return; the procedure was completed simply by dropping the receipt with your room number, received at check-in, into the box inside the elevator. A comfortable hotel, packed with free services, and a comparatively late check-out to some other hotels… it feels almost criminal that we didn’t find out about this hotel earlier.

If a hotel is just a place to return to sleep at the end of the day, Super Hotel Premier Osaka Hommachi Ekimae is undoubtedly a hotel that will make you want to return to sleep, even after your holiday is over.

Address: Osaka-fu, Osaka-shi, Nishi-ku, Nishihonmachi 1-5-10
大阪府大阪市西区西本町1-5-10
Check-in: 3:00 p.m.
Check-out: 11:00 a.m.

title: Final Fantasy Fat Chocobo Curry coming to fill up fans, even if they can’t attend Fan Festival
description: Instant curry endorsed by the heftiest of Final Fantasy’s avian mounts. Instant ramen may be Japan’s most famous savior of hungry people who don’t want to do any real cooking, but it’s not the only option for when you find yourself in those circumstances. The country also has instant curry that comes in pouches you […]
content:
Instant curry endorsed by the heftiest of Final Fantasy’s avian mounts.

Instant ramen may be Japan’s most famous savior of hungry people who don’t want to do any real cooking, but it’s not the only option for when you find yourself in those circumstances. The country also has instant curry that comes in pouches you heat up, either in the microwave or in a pot of boiling water, and can then pour over rice for a hot meal in just a fraction of the amount of time it would take to cook curry the conventional way.

There’s a lot of variety within the instant curry pouch world too, with various levels of spiciness, as well as different seasonings and key ingredients. As of this month, there’s even Final Fantasy instant curry, personally endorsed by none other than that most gastronomically motivated of recurring creatures, the Fat Chocobo! Specifically, it’s the chubby version of the franchise’s winged mount that appears in Final Fantasy XIV that’s giving this instant curry its sign of approval.

With Chocobos having features reminiscent of ostriches, hawks, and chickens, there’s sometimes debate among fans about whether or not the creatures are edible, but so far Final Fantasy XVI is the only game in the series with explicit mentions of people eating Chocobos. Final Fantasy XIV takes place in an entirely different world, one with no known instances of chocobo consumption by humans despite having the largest variety of in-game food items of any installment in the franchise. So while the Final Fantasy XIV Fat Chocobo Curry (to use the product’s full name) does have pieces of chicken in it, publisher Square Enix isn’t pushing this as a chance to taste chocobo meat in the real world, but instead as a rich, mild-spiciness curry “in the image of the Fat Chocobo,” with its unique yellow roux meant to remind fans of the chocobo’s canary-colored feathers.

The Fat Chocobo Curry is set to be offered for sale on-site at the upcoming Final Fantasy XIV Fan Festival Tokyo event on October 31 and November 1, but it will also be purchasable through the Square Enix online shop here, priced at 1,080 yen (US$6.80) Will it prove to be as tasty as the Resident Evil or Attack on Titan curry? We won’t know until after online sales officially start on October 16.

title: Japanese milk carton cakes are a genius idea that the world needs to know about
description: We’ve got all the details on where to find them, and how to eat them. There are many, many supermarket chains in Japan, but one of the most popular is Gyomu Super. Colloquially known as “Gyo-su”, this chain is designed for gyomu, or business use, so it’s stocked with bargain bulk buys that are commonly […]
content:
We’ve got all the details on where to find them, and how to eat them.

There are many, many supermarket chains in Japan, but one of the most popular is Gyomu Super. Colloquially known as “Gyo-su”, this chain is designed for gyomu, or business use, so it’s stocked with bargain bulk buys that are commonly purchased by restaurant owners, but it’s just as popular with regular customers and households looking to save money.

▼ Gyomu Super

Right now, the chain is in the spotlight on social media, thanks to a surprise product that not a lot of people know about: milk carton desserts. Gyomu Super actually sells around 10 varieties of these milk carton desserts, which pack around a kilo (2.2 pounds) of dessert into every carton. It’s a clever and compact way to serve up a big dessert, and now that a new Mitsuimo Cake has been added to the range for autumn, it was the perfect time for us to head out and try it.

Mitsuimo (literally “honey potato”) refers to sweet potatoes that become especially sweet and syrupy when cooked, with a moist and sticky texture. At first glance, you might think this carton contains Mitsuimo milk, if such a thing were to exist, but a closer look reveals this really is a cake, with the word “ケーキ” (“cake”) clearly printed on the packaging.

A cake in a carton sounds like a difficult thing to eat, but thankfully the pack comes with instructions on how to release the dessert from its packaging.

▼ First, open the entire thing up top so you can see into the carton…

▼…then tip it on its side and jiggle the dessert out onto a plate.

▼ Milk carton…

▼ …dessert!

▼ The cake slid out with a whoosh, surprising us with its presence.

▼ It was so golden and gleaming that it kind of looked like a gold bar.

Grabbing a knife, it slid through the dessert like butter, so we could easily cut a piece off and present it on a plate of its own.

After slicing, the dessert really began to resemble a cake, and when we tasted it, it had a rich sweetness and a sticky, dense texture, while being soft and jiggly at the same time. It was far more delicious than we thought it would be, with a texture like purin (Japanese pudding) but the taste of sweet potato.

Although it was tasty, the sweetness was quite strong, so it would be impossible for us to finish the whole carton as is. Thankfully, the pack comes with a few alternative ideas, like French Toast and Ice Cream Sandwiches, which both looked fantastic, but we decided to try their suggestion to use it as a spread.

Simply toast a thick slice of bread until golden brown, then spread on a layer of cream cheese and some of the Mitsuimo Cake.

▼ Since the Mitsuimo Cake is soft, it can be spread on toast like jam or butter.

This was a taste sensation. The rich sweetness of the sweet potato complemented the fresh tang of cream cheese to create a fantastic dessert-like treat. Great for breakfast or as a snack, this is something we could happily eat every day.

▼ Who knew carton cake on toast could be a thing?

The Mitsuimo Cake costs 537 yen (US$3.39), and with 7–8 servings in a pack, this was great value for money. The fact that it’s made domestically at a  factory Japan is another nice selling point.

▼ Once you’ve been initiated into the world of milk carton cakes, you’ll be keen to explore other options, like this Peach Jelly.

▼ Two quick and easy ways to serve up sweets at a gathering.

The only problem with the carton desserts is finding them. We found ours after visiting three different Gyomu Super branches, as they were so popular they’d already sold out. So if you do come across them, don’t hesitate to pick one up, so you too can fall in love with the wonders of Japan’s milk carton cakes.

title: Giant wagashi cushions will turn your home sweet home into home sweet Japanese sweets home
description: Nitori lets you cuddle up with taiyaki, dorayaki, and more. Japan has a lot of wise attitudes about food, and perhaps one of the most sensical of all is that dessert aesthetics are important. Sweets are a discretionary part of the diet, something eaten for enjoyment rather than nutrition, so if you can enjoy both […]
content:
Nitori lets you cuddle up with taiyaki, dorayaki, and more.

Japan has a lot of wise attitudes about food, and perhaps one of the most sensical of all is that dessert aesthetics are important. Sweets are a discretionary part of the diet, something eaten for enjoyment rather than nutrition, so if you can enjoy both the way they taste and the way they look, that’s double the fun.

Now Japanese housewares chain Nitori has extended that line of thinking, since if Japanese sweets look nice as food, they should look nice as part of your home’s interior decorations too, right?

That’s the logical conclusion being applied to Nitori’s Mochimochi Cushion line, with designs that apply wagashi (Japanese sweets) styling to mochimochi (“squeezably soft”) cushions. For example, at the end of a long, hard day at work or school, you could come home, plop yourself down on the couch, and curl up with the Taiyaki Mochimochi Cushion. The taiyaki, a pancake-like cake baked on a special grill into the shape of a fish with sweet red beans or other sweet fillings, is one of Japan’s most beloved wagashi varieties, and Nitori’s designers have done an amazing job recreating it in cushion form.

▼ Nitori taiyaki cushion

▼ Actual taiyaki

But there’s much more to the world of wagashi than just taiyaki, and Nitori actually has three other Japanese sweets cushions to fill your home with too (well, maybe two and a half others, depending on how you want to count one of them).

First up we have a dorayaki cushion, which draws its inspiration from the sandwiched sweet of two circular cakes with sweet red beans between.

▼ Dorayaki

▼ Dorayaki cushion

Then there’s the kuri manju cushion, modeled after a manju (steamed cake) with a chestnut (kuri) filling. Kuri manju are often oblong in shape and have the kanji character for kuri (栗) seared into the dough, and Nitori follows both design cues for its cushion.

▼ There’s an actual kuri manju in the wrapper in front of the cushion in this photo.

And last, there’s the Waffle Mochimochi Cushion.

This is what that “maybe two and a half other wagashi cushions” part was about. Waffles themselves, obviously, aren’t an indigenous part of Japanese cuisine. However, rather than being large enough to eat with a knife and fork, cooked to a light crisp, and drizzled with maple syrup. “waffles” in Japan are often smaller, softer, and folded around some sort of creamy filling.

Because of that, you could argue either way about whether or not Nitori’s waffle cushion represents Japanese dessert culture, but there’s no debating its cuteness, and it, like all of the other cushions, promises an invitingly mochimochi softness.

Nitori’s dorayaki and kuri manju cushions have been around for a while, but the taiyaki and waffle versions have just been added to the Mochimochi Cushion lineup. The taiyaki cushion is priced at 1,490 yen (US$9.40), while the others are 1,990 yen, and they’re all available through the Nitori online shop here.

title: 7-Eleven Japan now has Milk Miso Curry Ramen, but is that too much for one cup? [Taste test]
description: A special kind of regional ramen makes its 7-Eleven instant noodle debut, with help from the makers of Sapporo Ichiban. Nothing else has such a fundamental effect on the quality of ramen as the broth. Get the broth right, and you’re going to have at least an overall-good-tasting meal. If the broth is bad, though, […]
content:
A special kind of regional ramen makes its 7-Eleven instant noodle debut, with help from the makers of Sapporo Ichiban.

Nothing else has such a fundamental effect on the quality of ramen as the broth. Get the broth right, and you’re going to have at least an overall-good-tasting meal. If the broth is bad, though, it won’t matter what sort of noodles and toppings you have, since they’ll be soaked in subpar flavor.

With that in mind, 7-Eleven Japan is taking on a tough challenge with its latest instant ramen offering, since there’s a lot of complexity, and so also a lot of potential places to screw up, with the broth of the Milk Miso Curry Ramen.

This ramen didn’t come about by 7-Eleven just grabbing random things from around their kitchen and tossing them in the pot, though. Ramen with a mixed broth of miso, curry, and milk is a local specialty of Aomori Prefecture, located up at the northern tip of Japan’s main island of Honshu. This regional version hasn’t really spread to the rest of Japan, though, so 7-Eleven’s cup ramen version, which just recently went on sale, is going to be many people’s first encounter with milk miso curry ramen.

There’s an argument to be made, at the granular level, that the idea isn’t so strange. Ramen with miso-based broth has been popular for generations, and it’s a style especially loved by people in northern Japan. Ramen with a curry-based broth is less common, but not unheard of (though you’re more likely to run into curry udon noodles on restaurant menus than curry ramen). The island prefecture of Hokkaido, just north of Aomori, is known for “soup curry,” a variation with a more liquidy consistency than the thicker roux ordinarily used for Japanese curries. Some Japanese home chefs also like to add bit of milk to the pot when cooking curry or reheating leftover roux, to give it a richer flavor.

However, is 7-Eleven trying to be too clever by combining all three of those ingredients, miso, curry, and milk, in a single ramen broth? At the very least, it sounds like something that would require a delicate touch in balancing the flavors, but “delicate” isn’t usually a quality we associate with instant noodles.

In contrast to the complexity of the broth, making 7-Eleven’s Milk Miso Curry Ramen is simple. You just open the lid, fill the cup with boiling water up to the line marked on the inside of the container, wait four minutes for the contents to cook, and then stir in the broth packet.

Floating in the opaque brown broth were bean sprouts, wakame (seaweed), and ground meat. Appearance-wise, the broth looked pretty close to standard miso ramen broth, but it smelled different, with a buttery sweetness to the aroma that was wafting up as steam rose from the cup.

Using a spoon for extra classiness, our taste-testing reporter Yayoi Saginomiya took a sip of the broth, and much like with how it looks, the initial taste impression is strongly of miso. But as she went on eating, she could feel a building sensation of curry flavors coming on after the starting miso sensation.

However, Yayoi wouldn’t call any of the flavor profile’s notes “milky.” Moreso than milk, she felt like she was getting the flavor of butter. That might be because the broth uses powdered whole milk instead of liquid milk, something that’s probably unavoidable in order to meet the shelf-life expectations for instant ramen.

That’s not to say the broth is disappointing, though. Sure, in terms of flavor it may be more accurate to describe it as “miso curry butter ramen” than “milk miso curry ramen,” but it still tastes very good. With three ingredients that aren’t often combined together like this, there was a risk of a disorientating, discordant flavor as each of them tried to pull your taste buds in a different direction. 7-Eleven Japan, and their partners for this project at Sanyo Foods (makers of the Sapporo Ichiban instant ramen brand), though, have done an excellent job crafting a smooth, rich, and harmonious broth that’s miso-forward, with the curry coming on as a welcome guest and the milk helping tie everything together.

7-Eleven’s Milk Miso Curry Ramen may not be as dramatic-tasting as the concept sounds, but it is delicious, and if you’re a fan of miso ramen looking for a version of the broth with a twist to it, we highly recommended this.

title: Sushi Bus starts running in Japan, but is it a tourist trap or tourist must-do?
description: We take a trip on the world’s first conveyor belt sushi bus…and it’s like nothing we’ve ever seen before. Sushi and sightseeing tend to be at the top of the must-do list for many visitors to Japan, so what if you could combine the two and enjoy them at the same time? Well, now you […]
content:
We take a trip on the world’s first conveyor belt sushi bus…and it’s like nothing we’ve ever seen before.

Sushi and sightseeing tend to be at the top of the must-do list for many visitors to Japan, so what if you could combine the two and enjoy them at the same time? Well, now you can, thanks to the arrival of the Sushi Bus, a new two-decker restaurant bus that takes you on a tour around Tokyo while a conveyor belt filled with plates of sushi runs around the tables.

▼ In case you’re wondering, IBS Coach stands for International Business Solutions, not Irritable Bowel Syndrome.

Billed as the first bus in the world to have a sushi conveyor belt, there’s been a lot of buzz about the Sushi Bus, but does it live up to the hype? We stepped on board for a ride before tickets went on sale to find out if it was a tourist trap or a tourist must-do.

The first thing you’ll notice about the bus is its eye-catching exterior, with the entire vehicle wrapped in a giant image of two bright red tuna sushi pieces, which are said to be 12 metres (39 feet) long and 4 metres high. The bus is dubbed “Maguro-go” (“Tuna Vehicle“), with plans to introduce more buses to create a fleet from next year, and it’s a beautiful design that’ll make you feel like you’re entering a new world of sushi when you step on board.

Though the welcome sign is in English, the Sushi Bus caters to locals as well as international tourists – 70-percent of bookings in the first five days were made by Japanese people – and staff speak both English and Japanese.

▼ After making your way up a short flight of stairs, you’ll be surprised by the interior, which is like no other bus on the streets.

Running around the entire bus is a long conveyor belt, with lanterns giving the space a very Japanese vibe.

There are a variety of seating options on board the 20-seater bus, from two premium single seats at the very front…

▼ …through to a table for three…

▼…and tables for four…

▼ … and two.

▼ Every seat comes with seatbelts, which passengers are asked to wear while the bus is in operation.

As for the tables, they’re beautifully designed, at just the right height for eating, and with places in the centre console for holding the soy sauce bottle and your drinks.

Every passenger gets a free drink, with some of the choices being soft drinks, green tea, and beer.

The bus has an open-air rooftop, which gives you a fantastic view of the buildings as you glide through the streets. In inclement weather, the top closes up but it’s transparent so you can still see the Tokyo skyline.

Each tour lasts approximately 70 minutes, and takes you past some of the top spots around the city, including Tokyo Station…

▼ … Tokyo Tower…

▼ … the Imperial Palace…

▼…and the towering buildings of Ginza.

Tokyo really does look beautiful from the top of a double-decker bus, but you’ll soon find yourself looking away from the view when the sushi starts appearing on the belt.

The belt is surprisingly smooth, and there’s no fear of the sushi flying off, as the setup has been thoroughly tested to withstand even hard braking.

The all-you-can-eat extravaganza contains over a dozen sushi varieties, which may vary by day. When we visited we were able to enjoy offerings like:

▼ … egg…

▼ … crab…

▼ … salmon…

▼ … octopus…

▼ … tuna…

▼ … prawn…

▼ … squid…

▼… yellowtail…

▼ … and beef short ribs.

▼ There are also tubs filled with packs of pickled ginger and wasabi.

▼ Little plates are provided for you to empty the packs into.

▼ All the sushi is prepared in the kitchen downstairs…

▼ …and transported up to the dining area by way of a compact little elevator.

▼ Staff place the plates on the conveyor belt and keep an eye on things to make sure everything runs smoothly during the ride.

Throughout the entire tour, we couldn’t get over what we were seeing, not because of what was outside the window, but because of what was inside it.

▼ A constant stream of sushi surrounded us on the belt, like a sushi lover’s dream come to life.

While it looked wonderful, we were keen to know what the sushi actually tasted like, so we reached out and grabbed a plate of salmon from the belt.

▼ Beautifully presented on a Sushi Bus plate.

After stopping for a moment to take in the fact that we were eating sushi on a moving bus while people on the streets stared curiously at us, we dove in and found that the sushi was delicious.

Eager to try more, we grabbed the beef ribs, which were so flavourful that we found ourselves reaching for another serving immediately afterwards.

▼ Then we tried the tuna, which was another impressive offering.

Though you might think that sushi on a bus like this would be lacking in flavour, we were honestly surprised at how delicious it all was. The toppings were high quality and generously sized, and Sushi Bus says it places a lot of importance on its ingredients, sourcing them from a wholesaler at Toyosu Market who they have a business partnership with. The tuna, for instance, comes from different regions according to season, and each slice weighs 12 grams (0.4 ounces), which is about 1.5 times the amount you get at a regular conveyor belt sushi restaurant.

▼ The generous portions really do fill you up, and after five plates we were already feeling full.

▼ One of the passengers in the front seat, however, put us to shame with ten empty plates on the table.

The excitement of the tour is dialled up a notch with loud music and enthusiastic commentary from staff, who get everyone to look up at the bridges and highways that pass by within inches of the roof, giving you a unique feel for the city.

▼ The Sushi Bus is a feast for all the senses.

So…is it a tourist trap or a tourist must-do? Well, in our opinion, it’s a must-do. Sure, it’s touristy, and if you’re a local the price is pretty steep, at 16,000 yen (US$101) per person (or 22,000 yen for a premier front-row seat), but if you’re a tourist from overseas, or even outside of the prefecture, it’s an undeniably unique experience that’ll stay with you as a fun memory for years to come.

Plus, with all-you-can-eat sushi and a 70-minute trip around Tokyo that takes in some of the most iconic sights, it works out to be pretty good value, especially if you finish a lot of plates.

▼ Another bonus is the convenient pick-up and drop-off location at Marunouchi-Kajibashi Parking Lot, which is right next to Tokyo Station.

The Sushi Bus operates daily (with occasional closures for vehicle inspections and maintenance), and currently offers five tour times, with departures at 11 a.m., 1 p.m., 3 p.m., 5 p.m. and 7 p.m. Reservations can be made here, and the bus starts rolling around town from 10 October.

title: New Studio Ghibli notebooks are a beautiful reason to write and draw by hand [Photos]
description: Ghibli’s partnership with Japanese stationery brand Rollbahn expands to include three more theatrical anime. In the digital age, you don’t actually need to write by hand in order to put your thoughts into readable words, but many will say that nothing gets the creative juices flowing quite like putting pen to paper. And if artistic […]
content:
Ghibli’s partnership with Japanese stationery brand Rollbahn expands to include three more theatrical anime.

In the digital age, you don’t actually need to write by hand in order to put your thoughts into readable words, but many will say that nothing gets the creative juices flowing quite like putting pen to paper. And if artistic inspiration is the goal, being in the presence of great artwork might just make your creative process even juicier.

That philosophy is embodied by Studio Ghibli’s partnership with Rollbahn, a line of notebooks from Japanese stationery maker Delfonics. With so many memorable anime in the Ghibli filmography, the collaboration couldn’t cover all of them at once, and the line is now ready to expand with three new notebook designs, including some that don’t always get a lot of attention in the Ghibli merch world.

Starting with an unquestioned classic, though, is the new notebook saluting Castle in the Sky/Laputa. The stylized cover depicts Pazu’s daily routine of climbing onto his roof and greeting the morning (and the local flocks of birds) with a song from his trumpet.

Next we have a council of tanuki from Pom Poko, who’ve assembled to discuss how to deal with human encroachment into their living spaces, with the group expressing their approval of reviving the art of shapeshifting in order to walk among Tokyoites and observe their ways.

And finally, Tales from Earthsea, the most-maligned of Ghibli’s major theatrical releases, actually gets some love with a gorgeous cover showing Arren communing with a very important dragon in his life.

Studio Ghibli and Rollbahn are both famous for being very detail-oriented, and the notebooks have a number of thoroughly thought-out design elements. A thick, high-quality paper is used to resist ink bleeding or writing on the page’s opposite side from showing through. The pages all have a grid pattern, making them usable for writing or diagramming, and each page is perforated as well, allowing for a clean tear-out if you need to pass it off to someone else. A clear pocket at the back of the notebook also gives you a place to store any supplementary slips of paper you might need to keep nearby.

A cloth strap helps keep the book snugly closed while you’ve got it stashed in your bag when out and about, and even the colors of the binding rings and reflective text on the front are subtly differentiated to best coordinate with each cover design.

In addition to the three brand-new notebooks above, the Ghibli Rollbahn line has over a dozen different other designs for fans of My Neighbor Totoro, Spirited Away, Howl’s Moving Castle, and more, though the older notebooks fluctuate in and out of availability based on current inventory levels.

Each of the notebooks is priced at 1,430 yen (US$9.40) and can be ordered through the online store of Studio Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku here.

title: Starbucks Japan releases new Halloween Frappuccino and drinkware, but are they worth buying this year?
description: We find out if double the cats makes for double deliciousness. While it might feel like Halloween is creeping up on us now that we’re in October, at Starbucks in Japan the festivities have already leapt up at us, with the release of a special Halloween treat called the Blackberry Yoghurt Frappuccino. Designed around the […]
content:
We find out if double the cats makes for double deliciousness.

While it might feel like Halloween is creeping up on us now that we’re in October, at Starbucks in Japan the festivities have already leapt up at us, with the release of a special Halloween treat called the Blackberry Yoghurt Frappuccino.

Designed around the theme of “Halloween Purple Cat in Mystery Forest”, where a “Phantom Purple Cat” lures you into the forest, feline motifs are key to the celebrations this year, even in the drinkware range.

▼ The purple kitty is being hidden around stores, with pawprints leading to its secret location.

With both the drink and the drinkware released at stores in Japan on 9 October, our resident Starbucks expert K. Masami decided to go all in on the feline frivolity by purchasing one of the cutest goods in the range, the Cat Glow in the Dark Double Wall Heat-Resistant Glass Cup, and asking staff to serve the Frappuccino inside it.

▼ The result turned out to be one of the cutest things she’s ever seen.

While the cup is incredibly cute, with phosphorescent sprinkles in the base and a cat with bat wings reaching for the stars, the drink itself is just as adorable. Giving it its charm is the chocolate topper, in the shape of cat ears, with two varieties to choose from – “black” or “white”.

Though she initially wanted to go for black ears, which are decidedly more spooky, Masami instead opted for white, in honour of her white cat.

Masami’s feline has her so under its spell that even her drink choices are decided by it.

▼ You…will..adore…meeee…ow”

As an ardent lover of cats and yoghurt Frappuccinos, this drink had all the elements of a dream scanrio for Masami, but what she really wanted to know was… would it taste as good as it looks?

Taking a sip, Masami’s palate was immediately enthralled by the flavours. The tartness of the berries and yoghurt made it refreshing and easy to drink, and there were even tiny blueberry pieces swimming around in the mix, adding exciting bursts of texture. The creamy milk and blackberry sauce gave every sip a delicious richness, and the balance was superbly well-crafted, making for a delicious Frappuccino.

While she was very impressed with the drink, Masami was even more impressed by the effect of the cat ears on top, which added so much cuteness that it seemed to make every mouthful even more delicious.

Both the drink and the drinkware are definitely worth buying, and the Frappuccino tasted so good that Masami vowed to return again to try it, perhaps next time with black cat ears, and without publishing it online, so her white kitty doesn’t find out about it. She’s also keen to try it with one of the recommended customisations, like chocolate chips, for added taste and texture.

▼ Always watching and reading your stories, Masami.

The Halloween Frappuccino, and the limited-edition seasonal drinkware, are available for a limited time, and only while stocks last, so be sure to get in quick to enjoy the celebrations.

title: Burger King serves up Pickleball Burgers in Japan, with a tasty nod to the number 11
description: Limited-edition exclusive comes with free goods and special prizes. Burger King is always looking for ways to stand out from the competition in Japan, and right now it’s doing exactly that with the release of a brand new Pickleball Burger. Created as part of the chain’s ongoing efforts to promote pickleball in Japan, where it’s […]
content:
Limited-edition exclusive comes with free goods and special prizes.

Burger King is always looking for ways to stand out from the competition in Japan, and right now it’s doing exactly that with the release of a brand new Pickleball Burger.

Created as part of the chain’s ongoing efforts to promote pickleball in Japan, where it’s sponsored the Pickleball Japan Federation since 2025, there are two varieties in the lineup – the Pickleball Burger and the Chicken Pickleball Burger.

Each burger contains a whopping 11 pickles, as a nod to the scoring in the game, where the first player to reach 11 points wins.

Everyone’s a winner with these two burgers, as they both feature a special creamy dill sauce that balances the refreshing aromas of dill and lemon in every serving. The standard version serves up two of the chain’s signature flame-grilled beef patties, with lettuce and onions, while the chicken version swaps the beef for a chicken patty that’s crispy on the outside and juicy on the inside.

As an added bonus, the chain is giving away a free original pickleball paddle keychain for every burger purchased, although stocks are limited so you’ll want to get in quick to receive them.

Pickleball lovers and those who are new to the sport can also enjoy some extra fun with a special pickleball game on Burger King Japan’s official app. Win at the game and you’ll be rewarded with discount coupons, and if you happen to achieve a special, super-rare winning animation, you’ll automatically be entered into a lottery to win an original Burger King paddle.

The game runs from 1 p.m. on 9 October until 11:59 p.m. on 15 October. As for the burgers, they’ll be available at store locations nationwide, excluding the Kansai International Airport Terminal and racecourse branches, from 9 October. The beef Pickleball burger will be on the menu at 1,490 yen (US$9.43), or 1,790 yen as a set, while the chicken will be priced at 690 yen, or 990 yen as a set, and they’ll both be on the menu in limited quantities while supplies last.
